opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot. The core tension is that different downstream tasks want very different things from a representation. If you're doing something like object classification, you generally want invariance: you want the representation to throw away things like the exact pose, the lighting, the precise location of the object, because those are nuisance factors for that task. But if you're doing something like depth estimation, object counting, or robotic manipulation, those exact details are the signal. So a single flat representation trained with one objective is almost forced to make a trade-off, and whatever invariances you bake in during pretraining end up helping some tasks and hurting others.

Hierarchical representations offer a natural way out of that dilemma. The idea is that you don't commit to a single level of abstraction. Lower levels of the hierarchy can preserve fine-grained, local, spatially precise information, while higher levels progressively abstract away detail and capture more semantic, global, and often longer-timescale structure. Then a downstream task can draw on whichever level, or combination of levels, carries the information it needs, rather than being stuck with whatever the pretraining objective decided was important.

This connects to how we've been thinking about joint-embedding predictive architectures. In a JEPA, you're predicting in representation space rather than pixel space, so the model gets to decide what's predictable and discard what's unpredictable noise. That's really nice for learning semantic features, but it does raise the question of how much low-level detail you keep. A hierarchical JEPA lets you make predictions at multiple levels: short-horizon, fine-grained predictions at lower levels, and longer-horizon, more abstract predictions at higher levels. That's also important for planning and world modeling. If you want an agent to plan over long horizons, you can't do it at the level of individual pixels or individual motor commands. You want to plan with abstract states and then refine downward.

I'll add a caveat, though. Hierarchy isn't a free lunch. Getting each level to actually specialize, rather than collapse or redundantly encode the same information, is non-trivial, and there are open questions about how to train these levels jointly and how to evaluate whether you've got the right abstractions. But conceptually, I think hierarchy is one of the most promising ways to reconcile those conflicting requirements, because it lets one model serve tasks that need invariance and tasks that need precise detail, instead of forcing that choice up front.

r001.rationale: The response explains that higher levels abstract away detail while preserving information useful to a task, and that downstream tasks can select levels carrying what they need.

r002.rationale: It says a single flat representation must trade off between tasks with different information needs, so no one representation suits all tasks.

r003.rationale: It proposes that tasks can draw on different hierarchy levels, including fine-grained lower levels and more abstract higher levels.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is really at the heart of the problem. If you think about what you want out of a representation, different tasks pull you in very different directions. Take something like semantic classification, where you want the representation to throw away a lot of information. You don't care whether the dog is on the left or the right side of the image, or exactly what the lighting is like. You just want "dog." But then take a task like depth estimation or instance segmentation, or really anything involving control or planning in the physical world. There, you need exactly that fine-grained, spatially local information you were trying to discard a moment ago. So if you train a single flat representation, you end up making a trade-off, and the usual symptom is that you get something that's decent at semantics but mediocre at the lower-level stuff, or vice versa.

The way I think about hierarchy is that it lets you stop pretending one level of abstraction has to serve everyone. At the lower levels of the hierarchy, the representations stay close to the input. They're spatially grounded, they preserve detail, they change quickly over time if you're dealing with video. As you move up, you're increasingly abstracting over space and over time, so you're representing things like objects, their relationships, maybe what's going to happen over the next several seconds rather than the next frame. And the point is that a downstream task can tap into whichever level matches its information requirements. A robot deciding where to put its gripper reads from a lower level. A system deciding what the overall plan should be reads from a higher one.

What's nice about this from a learning perspective, and this is something that comes up a lot in the JEPA line of work, is that prediction gets easier when you let it happen at the right level. Predicting every pixel of the future is basically impossible because the world is stochastic, and you waste all your capacity modeling noise. But predicting a more abstract representation of the future is much more tractable, because the abstraction has already dropped the unpredictable details. So hierarchy isn't just about serving multiple tasks after the fact. It's also what makes the self-supervised objective itself well-posed at each level. Each level predicts at a horizon and granularity that's actually learnable given what it keeps and what it throws away.

And honestly, I think this is also closer to how we'd want a system to reason. When you plan to go make coffee, you don't plan it in terms of individual muscle contractions. You plan it at a coarse level and then refine as you go. The hierarchy is what gives you that ability to move between levels of abstraction, and I think that's where a lot of the interesting work is right now, in figuring out how to learn those levels jointly rather than hand-designing them.

r001.rationale: It explains that semantic classification discards details such as position and lighting while retaining the information needed to identify “dog.”

r002.rationale: It says a single flat representation must trade off between tasks with different information needs, often performing well on one type and poorly on another.

r003.rationale: It states that downstream tasks can use whichever hierarchy level matches their information requirements, with examples of lower- and higher-level use.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that different tasks require different levels of abstraction. If you’re trying to recognize an object, you might want a representation that’s invariant to its precise position or to some of its visual details. But if you’re trying to manipulate that object, its position and geometry suddenly become really important. So information that’s a nuisance for one task can be essential for another.

A hierarchy gives you a way to accommodate both. At lower levels, you can preserve more of the local, detailed information, while higher levels capture more abstract, semantic information. Then a downstream task can draw on the level—or combination of levels—that’s appropriate for it. You don’t have to force a single representation to discard information and preserve it at the same time.

The interesting challenge is how to learn that hierarchy so that those different levels actually capture useful abstractions, rather than assuming that simply making a network deeper will give you that structure.

r001.rationale: It explains that abstraction depends on the task: object recognition can discard position or visual detail, while manipulation needs that information.

r002.rationale: It says a single representation should not be forced to discard and preserve information at the same time.

r003.rationale: It states that downstream tasks can draw on the hierarchy level or combination of levels suited to them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that different tasks require different levels of abstraction. If you’re recognizing an object, you might want a representation that’s invariant to its position or the lighting. But if you’re trying to manipulate that object, its position is precisely the information you need. So an invariance that helps one task can actually hurt another.

A hierarchy gives us a way to retain those different kinds of information at different levels. Lower levels can capture more local, detailed information, while higher levels capture more abstract, semantic information. Then a downstream task can draw on the level—or combination of levels—that’s appropriate for it, rather than forcing every task to use a single representation with the same invariances.

r002.rationale: It says task needs differ and argues against forcing every task to use one representation with the same invariances.
